caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No.70 of 1986.
lawyer:
Lutfor Rahman Mondal with Kohinoor Hossain Khan and Md Abdus Samad Kamal, Advocates — For the Appellants. 
Moazzem Hossain, Deputy Attorney-General — For the Government (Respondent No.1) 
Maksudor Rahman with Mir Hashmat Ali, Advocates — For the Respondent No.2-4, 6-19, 22-24, 26-28, 31 and 37.
parties:
Roushan Ara Bewa and others ------ Appellants
Vs.
People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
"That upon grounds stated in the plaint a decree be passed declaring that the whole proceedings in exchange case No. 1/Naogaon of 1968-69 was tainted with fraud and that the power of Attorney set up by defendants 1 to 8 in respect of the properties of schedule "A" of the plaint was forged and fabricated and, as such, deed No. 29982 of 1968-69 executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi is void and of no legal effect." 

 4. The suit was contested by defendant Nos.  1 to 12, by the Government of Bangladesh, Defendant No. 13 and by defendant Nos.  23 to 32 and 38 by filing 3 separate written statements. Defendant Nos. 1 to 12 contested the suit by denying the material averments made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the plaintiffs have no cause of action for the suit, that the plaintiffs have got no locus standi to file the suit, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and that the plaintiffs were not entitled to the reliefs prayed for. Their case, in short, is that the properties described in schedule ''A'' to the plaint previously belonged to the Hindu owners Khagendra Nath Roy, Mohendra Nath Roy, Manindra Nath Roy and his three brothers; that those owners of the properties left for India for good some time before 1964 and while in India they intended to exchange the said properties with suitable properties in India; that pursuant to negotiation between the parties for exchange of the said properties described in schedule ''A'' to the plaint with the Indian properties of Kazi Moshitullah, Kazi Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum described in schedule ''B'' of the power of attorney, the said Khagendra Nath Roy and others executed a power of attorney in June, 1964 for the purpose of completion of exchange document in this country in respect of the properties of schedule ''A'' to the plaint and they appointed defendant No. 9 Chowdhury Mohammad Ali as their constituted attorney and the said Kazi Moshitullah, Kazi Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum executed and registered a deed of exchange in India in favour of the said Khagendra Nath Roy and others in respect of their Indian properties; that the said power of attorney was duly re-stamped and revalidated; that the said exchangee Kazi Moshitullah died in 1971 leaving behind defendant Nos.  1 to 8 as his heirs; that for regularisation of the exchange between the parties, Exchange case No. 1 /Naogaon/ 1968-69 was started and after due inquiry and report regarding the genuineness of the exchange by competent officers of the Government, the exchange in question was regularised and the transfer deed relating to the said exchange was executed and registered by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi; that the other defendants are transferees from the exchangees; that some of the land out of theland described in Schedule ''A'' to the plaint were wrongly listed as enemy properties in the office of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Naogaon but as a matter of fact those were not taken in possession by the SDO and the plaintiffs obtained some lease documents purporting to show lease in their favour in respect of "B" schedule properties; but those documents were simply paper transactions and that the plaintiffs have instituted the suit without any subsisting interest whatsoever in the suit properties only to harass the defendants on false and concocted allegations. 

 5. Defendant No. 13, the Government of Bangladesh, by filing a separate written statement contested the suit stating that the plaintiffs have no cause of action for the suit, that they have got no locus standi to file that suit as they have or had no right, title, Interest or possession in the suit land or in any portion thereof; that the properties in question belonged to Hindu owners Khagendra Nath Roy and others, that the said owners while in possession of the said properties intended to exchange the properties with suitable properties in India, that there was negotiation of exchange with the Indian properties of Kazi Moshitullah, Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum and they executed a general power of attorney in June, 1964 in favour of Chowdhury Mohammad Ali for the purpose of completion of the exchange document in this country in respect of the properties described in schedule ''A'' to the plaint and in lieu thereof the said Kazi Moshitullah and Kazi Badiuzzaman and Roushan Ara Begum executed and registered an exchange deed in India in favour of the said Khagendra Nath Roy and others in respect of their Indian properties: that for regularisation of the exchange, Exchange case No. 1/Naogaon/1968-69 was started and after verification, enquiry and report regarding the genuineness of the exchange by competent officers of the Government the exchange in question was regularised and a transfer deed relating to the said exchange properties was executed and registered by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi in accordance with law. 

 6. Defendant Nos.   23 to 32 and 38 also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement supporting the case of contesting defendants and stating further that they have purchased some land from the aforesaid exchanges. 

 7. At the trial the plaintiffs examined 7 PWs including plaintiff No. 3 and plaintiff No. 5 and the defendants examined 2 witnesses including the Attorney , Chowdhury Mohammad Ali PW 1. Abdul Latif Khan is a Law Clerk of Naogaon Collectorate who produced the record of Exchange case No. 1/Naogaon/1968. PW 2 Md. Azimuddin Sarder is plaintiff No. 3 who deposed on behalf of the plaintiffs; he stated that the plaintiffs used to possess the "B" schedule land as borgader and the remaining lands of schedule ''A'' were also cultivated by other Borgaders; that the plaintiffs used to deliver the borga crops to the employees of the owners of the land and then to the Chairman, Union Parishad, Badalgachi. The lands were treated as vested properties and they took lease of ''B'' schedule properties from the office of the Sub-Divisional Officer, Naogaon. He stated that coming to know about the filing of the exchange case they filed objection in the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi and there was inquiry and report by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) and on their further prayer there was another inquiry by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (General); but since there was no decision taken by the authority they approached the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reform. He further stated that the exchangees had no properties in India and asserted that the exchange document was a fraudulent one. In his cross-examination he admitted that they filed objection against the regularisation of the exchange case and there was hearing of the matter in presence of their appointed pleader. He admitted that he did not know about the Indian properties of Moshitullah and he heard that Moshitullah was a Constable. He admitted that they have no DCR since 1979. He could not say the area of the exchanged land nor he could state the plot number in his possession. He also admitted that he had no personal knowledge as to whether the exchangees executed and registered any document in India in favour of Hindu owners. PW 3 Asiruddin Mondal is plaintiff No. 5. He stated that the suit land was declared as enemy property and they took separate lease, but in cross-examination he could not say the dag number and area of the land and he admitted that his yearly lease was not renewed since 1387 BS (1977-78). PW 4 Abdur Rahman Sarder stated that the plaintiffs possessed the suit land by taking lease from the Enemy Property Authorities. But in his cross-examination he could not say the names and numbers of the plaintiffs nor he could say about the area of land or plot number of the land possessed by the plaintiffs. PW 5 Jasimuddin Ahmed stated that PW 2 and PW 3 along with other plaintiffs possessed the suit land. But in his cross-examination he could not say the number of the plaintiffs except 2 nor could he say in which mouza or plot number the plaintiff possessed. PW 6 Amir Ali Khondker has produced a document alleged to be executed by Debendra, Jogendra, Hemendra and Rabindra on 8-1-51 in favour of his father Abbas Ali. He stated that the plaintiff Azimuddin (Plaintiff No. 3) and a few Hindus possessed the suit land. In his cross-examination he submitted that he did not know the plot number of the land in possession of Azimuddin. PW 7 Md Shah Jahan Ali is the Tahsildcr of Badalgachi in respect of enemy properties; he stated that some of the properties were released from the enemy properties but lease in respect of some other properties are continuing. But he did not bring any document in support of his statement and he filed a document relating to order of release Ext.B(1). In his cross-examination he admitted that in view of memo No. 131 dated 19-3-79 those properties were released and thereafter no lease was granted in respect of those properties. DW 1 is Chowdhury Mohammad Ali (defendant No. 9), the constituted attorney for execution of exchange document. He stated that the properties belonged to Hemendra Nath Roy and others and he knew Kazi Moshitullah and defendant Nos.  1 and 2 who had these properties in India. He further stated that Kazi Moshitullah and 2 others exchanged their Indian properties with the properties of Hemendra Nath Roy and others and the aforesaid Muslim party transferred their Indian properties in favour of the aforesaid Hindu party by a registered document dated 18-6-64. He further stated that the aforesaid Hindu party executed a power of attorney on 18-6-64 which was authenticated by a Magistrate of Balurghat in India. He proved the signature of the Hindu party on the power of attorney by which he was appointed the attorney. He further stated that he filed an application before the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi in 1968 for regularisation of exchange and the plaintiffs raised certain objections against the regularisation of the exchange document and there was inquiry and after rejecting the objection of the plaintiffs the document was executed by the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi which was registered on 11-8-76. Thereafter some of the properties covered by the exchange deed which were previously declared as enemy properties were released from the enemy list. He denied that the plaintiffs were borgaders under the original Hindu owners and stated that the plaintiffs possessed some of the land by taking lease from the Enemy Property Authorities. In his cross-examination he denied that the concerned officers have filed false and biased report in respect of the exchange. He also denied that the Muslim party had no property in India. He further stated that after registration of the exchange deed the heirs of Kazi Moshitullah got possession of 60/70 bighas of land through a Magistrate. He also denied that the plaintiffs were borgaders under the original owners or they were still in possession by taking lease from the enemy property authorities. DW 2 Ahmed Ali Sardar is defendant No.  25. He supported the case of the exchangees and he further stated that his father and uncle purchased 23.10 acres of land from Moshitullah and obtained a registered deed of release from defendant No. 1. He further stated that his father purchased 18.42 acres of land from defendant Nos.  1 and 2 by a registered kabala dated 17-7-73 and they also sold 13.77 acres of land to his uncle Abdul Hamid on the same day; that subsequently the children of defendant No. 1 executed two deeds of lease in respect of those two sales on 19-7-79. In his cross-examination he denied that his father and his uncle Abdul Hamid did not purchase any land. 

 9. Mr Lutfor Rahman Mondal, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-appellants, has taken us through the plaint, written statements, deposition of the witnesses and the relevant documentary evidence and submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in holding that the exchange in question was not genuine. The learned Advocate has also submitted that the suit was not maintainable at the instance of the plaintiffs inasmuch as they have no right, title, interest and even possession in the land described in schedule ''B'' to the plaint. The learned Advocate further has taken us through the different circulars issued by the Government from time to time to regularise exchange document and submitted that after proper inquiry the Deputy Commissioner, Rajshahi certified the transaction as a genuine exchange and pursuant to that the exchange deed in question was executed and registered. 

 13. As to possession, the plaintiffs asserted that they are in possession of ''B'' schedule land. But PWs 2 and 3 failed to give the particulars of the land in their possession. On the other hand, DW 1 Chowdhury Mohammad Ali although admitted that some of the plaintiffs possessed some land by taking lease from the Enemy Property authorities, stated that after execution of the transfer deed Ext.A(5), the exchangees got possession of 60/70 bighas of land through a Magistrate and apart from those lands late Moshitullah was in possession of the remaining land. From the above evidence it is clear that the plaintiffs or any one of them had no possession in any portion of the property in question since 1979 when the portion of the property taken over as enemy properties was released. 

 14. The plaintiffs also asserted that they were borgaders under the previous Hindu owners and subsequently became annual lessees under the enemy property authorities. Plaintiff No. 3, deposing as PW 2 on behalf of all the plaintiffs, alone stated that the plaintiffs were borgader in respect of ''B'' schedule properties. But no other witness corroborated him on the point of borga cultivation, not even plaintiffs No. 5 who deposed as PW 3. PW 3 simply stated that the suit land was declared enemy property and they individually took lease; but he admitted that after 1384 BS (1977-78) he would not renew his lease. Thus, although the plaintiffs asserted that they were borgaders in respect of ''B'' schedule land they failed to establish that they took lease of 32.50 acres of land of ''B'' schedule. On the other hand, the relevant lease orders and duplicate carbon receipts show that only four of the plaintiffs took annual lease of 4.25 acres of land out of schedule ''B'' and, for that matter, out of the lands of schedule ''A'' and that too came to an end in 1979. We, therefore, find no merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents that the plaintiffs are still in possession and the suit at their instance was maintainable. 

 27. Let me now see whether the Deputy Commissioner was authorised under the law to transfer entire suit land showing different quantum of lands in the respective share to defendant Nos. 1 to 8. The decision of the then Dhaka High Court in the said case relied on by the Deputy Commissioner was on the interpretation of the provision of section 20(2) (b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 wherein there was no definition of the family. Accordingly, it was held that wife could retain khas land within the limit separately from her husband. It may be mentioned that the Deputy Commissioner by order dated 8-4-70 before coming into operation of President's Order 98 of 1972 held that wife could retain land separately from her husband relying on the said decision. So, the said order lost its force after coming into operation of President's Order 98 of 1972. In view of the definition of family in article 2(b) of President's Order 98 of 1972 already noticed the said decision has/had no manner of application at the time of execution of the said deed of transfer in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 to 8 by the Deputy Commissioner. It is also true that a minor can own land but the question is whether he could retain land in excess of the limit as a member of a family. We have already found that defendant No. 2 Kazi Badiuzzaman was a member of the same family with his father and mother and after death of his father with his mother and other heirs of his father. 

 28. Defendant Nos. 23 to 32 and 38 in their written statement and DW 2 Ahmed Ali Sardar, son of late Abdur Rahman Sardar, in his deposition claimed that late Abdur Rahman Sardar and his brother Abdul Hamid Sardar purchased 23.10 acres of the suit land from Kazi Moshitullah on the basis of sale deeds dated 18-1-1971 and the said deed was burnt in the Sub-Registrar's office in 1971. He further stated that Kazi Moshitullah then died and defendant No. 1 executed nadabi deed dated 22-1-1979 (Ext. A(2). He also stated that defendant Nos.  1 and 2 sold 18.42 acres of land to his father by sale deed dated 17-7-73 (Ext.A) and 13.77 acres of land to his uncle Abdul Hamid by sale deed 17-7-93 (Ext.A(4) and minor sons of defendant No. 1 executed and registered nadabi deeds dated 19-1-79 Ext.A(1) & A(3) confirming the aforesaid sales after they attained majority. Though in nadabi deed dated 22.1.1979 Ext.A(2) it has been admitted that late Abdur Rahman Sardar purchased 23.10 acres of land from Kazi Moshitullah and Roushan Ara by a registered sale deed dated 18-1-71 and the said sale deed was burnt in the Sub-Registrar Office during the war of liberation in 1971 but nothing has been produced to show that, in fact, such a deed of sale was executed and registered as claimed. The best evidence would have been the receipt granted by the Sub-Registrar Office after presentation for registration of the deed, for taking back the document after completion of registration in support of such a claim. In the absence of reliable proof of execution and registration of such a deed and burning of the Sub-Registrar Office in question and destruction of the alleged sale deed were admission in the said nadabi deed by one of the heirs of late Kazi Moshitullah cannot create any interest in the said land in favour of Abdur Rahman Sardar and his brother Abdul Hamid. It is well settled that a nadabi deed is not a deed of transfer and it alone cannot create any interest in favour of the recipient of the nadabi deed in respect of the land mentioned in the nadabi deed. I, therefore, find no basis for the claim that 23.10 acres of the suit land was sold to late Abdur Rahman Sardar and Abdul Hamid Sardar. Moreover at that time alleged exchange was not regularized. 

 29. Article 5 of President's Order 98 of 1972 provides that a family shall be deemed to be holding land in excess of 100 standard bighas if the aggregate of total quantity of land held by all members of the family on the date of submission of statement under article 7 together with the total quantity of land, if any transferred by them after the 20th day of February 1972 and before the date of submission of such statement exceeds one hundred standard bighas. Article 5A of President's Order 98 of 1972 provides that all transfers of land made by any member of a family, holding land in excess of one hundred standard bighas within the meaning of article 5 after the 15th day of August 1972 and before the date of submission of such statement under article 7 and also all such transfers, on or before that date without any registered deed shall be void. Article 6 gives option to such a family to select the lands to be surrendered and article 7 provides that head of such family shall submit statement by 31st January 1973 and government may extend the time limit. Article 8 provides that if the head of the family fails without any reasonable cause to submit the statement required under article 7 within the time he shall be punishable with imprisonment and/or fine and the land for which no statement has been made may be forfeited to the government and article 10 provides that excess land surrendered by a family shall vest in the government subject to the provision of article 11 providing for appeal and revision and under article 13 owner of such surrendered land will get compensation. 

 30. From the above provisions of President's Order 98 of 1972 it is clear that no family can hold land in excess of 100 standard bighas and all transfers made by such a family after 15 August 1972 and all transfers, made before that date without a registered deed shall be void. Though the defendants Nos.  1-12 in their written statement stated that defendant Nos.  1-8 transferred some land to defendant Nos.  9-12 without any particulars but no documents were produced or proved in court in support of such claim. Any such transfer if comes within the mischief of President's Order 98 of 1972 shall also be void. In that view of the law already noticed all the transfers by the defendant Nos.  1-8 by the deeds of sale Ext.A and A(1) and all the transfers admitted in the nadabi deeds Ext.A(1), A(2) and A(3) are void and those did not create any interest in the suit land in favour of late Abdur Rahman Sarder and defendant No. 23, Abdul Hamid or Abdur Rahman's heirs defendant Nos.  24-32 and 38. 

 33. Learned Advocate of the appellants submitted that the defendant Nos. 1-8 did not file any statement surrendering the excess land in pursuance of the undertaking furnished by them before the execution and registration of the deed of transfer in their favour by the Deputy Commissioner due to pendency of litigations. Their failure to submit statement to the appropriate revenue officer within the specified time brings them within the mischief of article 8 of President's Order 98 of 1972 and the entire land in question is liable to be forfeited. In view of the anomaly created in the said deed of transfer and in view of the fact that litigation is going on in respect of the suit property and in view of the fact that defendant No. 1 is a lady and other defendant Nos.  2-8 are her children and were minors at the relevant time and they all constituted one family and they were entitled to retain 100 standard bighas of land at the relevant time they should be allowed to retain 100 standard bighas of land and the appropriate revenue officer shall resume the balance quantum of suit ''A'' schedule land already vested in the government after giving an opportunity to the defendant Nos.  1-8 for expressing their option to select the lands to be surrendered and 100 standard bighas of land to be retained by them. Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Deputy Commissioner Naogaon to take steps to comply with the aforesaid direction.
